newsitem.title: USA: Aberdeen commander quits, adultery reported.
newsitem.headline: Aberdeen commander quits, adultery reported.

text.p: The commander of the U.S. Army's scandal-plagued Aberdeen Proving Ground, Maj. Gen. John Longhouser, is to retire, officials said on Tuesday, and the New York Times said he had admitted to an adulterous affair.

"He is retiring," said base spokesman John Yaquiant, who said he could not comment on the adultery report. A statement said Longhouser was stepping down "to spend more time with his family and other interests after 32 years in the Army."
Longhouser, 53, left as of Tuesday as head of the proving ground and commander of the Army's Test and Evaluation Command although his retirement takes effect on June 30, Yaquiant said.

The New York Times said on Tuesday, citing Pentagon officials, that Longhouser would retire at a lower rank after admitting he had an affair while separated from his wife about five years ago. Pentagon spokesmen said they could neither confirm nor deny the report and Longhouser's office at Aberdeen referred a request for comment to base spokesmen.

The newspaper said Longhouser, a two-star general, will retire at the rank of a one-star general, which will mean a reduction in his retirement benefits. It said the military had received an anonymous tip about him over a telephone hot line established after revelations of a sexual misconduct scandal at Aberdeen's Ordnance Centre and School, where 12 male trainers have been charged with preying on women recruits.

Yaquiant said Longhouser did not have direct disciplinary responsibilty for the Ordnance Centre and School, which is part of the Army's Training and Doctrine Command, a separate unit from the Test and Evaluation Command, but was responsible for convening courts martial to try those charged with crimes.
Longhouser's case involved a civilian in an affair that occurred before he arrived at Aberdeen, in September 1996, and while he was separated from his wife, the Times said.

Of the 12 Ordnance Centre and School trainers charged in a sexual misconduct investigation disclosed last November, four were found guilty of violations, two received discharges in lieu of court martial and six are still awaiting resolution.
Longhouser will be succeded on a temporary basis by Maj. Gen. George Friel, commander of the Army's Chemical and Biological Defence Command.
